name: eFFT (event-based FFT)
baseline: FFTW (fftw_plan_dft_2d, full N x N 2D FFT recomputed after every event or event packet)
workload: Incrementally maintaining the exact 2D FFT of an N x N event-camera frame (N = 16 to 256) as random single events (250 per iteration) or packets of 100 to 5000 events arrive, versus re-running a full FFTW 2D transform after each update.
claimed_speedup: Faster than FFTW for incremental event-stream updates: the README says FFTW3 'served as the benchmark for testing and evaluation' and the repo ships paired Google Benchmark cases (BenchmarkFeedWithEvents vs BenchmarkFeedWithEventsFFTW, BenchmarkFeedWithPackets vs BenchmarkFeedWithPacketsFFTW). No numeric result or speedup ratio is printed on any page I could open.
compiler_and_flags: Compiler not stated (CMake default toolchain). benchmarks target in the root CMakeLists.txt: -O3 -march=native -flto -funroll-loops -finline-functions -fomit-frame-pointer -ffast-math, defines NDEBUG, EIGEN_STACK_ALLOCATION_LIMIT=0 and EFFT_USE_FFTW3; C++17, Eigen >= 3.4, FFTW3 >= 3.3.8, Google Benchmark.
stars_or_usage: 23 stars, 2 forks; PyPI package efft; Docker image; TPAMI 2024 and JORS 2026 papers
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 on top of Eigen; frame size is a compile-time template parameter and must be a power of two (radix-2 tree); keeps a tree of intermediate matrices (about log2 N levels of N x N complex floats) so memory is well above one frame; single-precision complex (float) output; GPLv3 copyleft; Python bindings via nanobind. It is not a drop-in FFT: it only wins when the input changes by a few pixels between transforms (event streams) and needs one initial full transform.
caveats: (1) No benchmark numbers and no CPU model appear in the repo or on any page I could open; the TPAMI paper (doi 10.1109/TPAMI.2024.3422209), the JORS paper (doi 10.5334/jors.642), IEEE Xplore, PubMed and Zenodo are egress-blocked here. Only a WebSearch snippet of the paper abstract was seen (snippet only, not on benchmark_url): exactness PSNR > 55 dB and SSIM > 0.999, event processing time < 1 microsecond for packets of more than 40 events and < 0.5 microsecond for packets of more than 200 events at 128 x 128. That snippet states absolute eFFT times, not a ratio against FFTW. Retier to B if the TPAMI paper confirms the FFTW numbers. (2) The in-repo FFTW baseline is deliberately weak: initializeGroundTruth plans with FFTW_ESTIMATE | FFTW_UNALIGNED | FFTW_NO_SIMD | FFTW_PRESERVE_INPUT, uses double-precision complex while eFFT uses float, recomputes the whole N x N 2D transform for every single event, and getGroundTruthFFT() also copies and casts the whole N x N result to a float Eigen matrix each call while eFFT.getFFT() returns a const reference. Any speedup measured with this harness is inflated relative to a tuned FFTW (FFTW_MEASURE, SIMD, float, no copy). (3) Different problem from a plain FFT: incremental update after sparse input changes versus a from-scratch transform, so the comparison is only meaningful for event-stream use. (4) benchmark.cpp seeds events from std::random_device, so runs are not bit-reproducible. (5) Repo last commit date (2026-09-22) was read from the github.com commits page via WebFetch.

name: PFT (Partial Fourier Transform)
baseline: FFTW (real-to-complex 1D, FFTW_ESTIMATE), Intel MKL DFTI, FFTW pruned FFT, Goertzel algorithm
workload: Computing only M of the N Fourier coefficients of a real-valued time series (repo defaults N = 4194304, M = 131072; datasets are synthetic random vectors of power-of-two length, Urban Sound, Air condition and Stock series) and comparing against full FFTs from FFTW and MKL, FFTW pruned FFT and Goertzel.
claimed_speedup: Order of magnitude speedup for sufficiently small output sizes without sacrificing accuracy, outperforming FFTW, MKL, pruned FFT and Goertzel (KDD 2021 paper, arXiv 2008.12559). Text seen only as a WebSearch snippet of the paper abstract; it is not on any page I opened and I could not read the paper's tables.
tradeoffs: Approximate, not exact: error is selectable from e-1 to e-7 through precomputed polynomial coefficient files (src/precomputed). The sample code is written for real-valued input and a target output range centered at zero (the file header says a small modification removes this limit). Single precision throughout. Needs Intel MKL and IPP (mkl.h, mkl_dfti.h, ipp.h, ipps.h) plus fftw3.h. Gains only when M is much smaller than N (O(N + M log M) instead of O(N log N)). Research sample code, not a packaged library.
caveats: (1) Paper numbers, CPU model, compiler and flags were not obtainable: arXiv, dl.acm.org, openreview and yongchanpark.github.io (the author PDF) are egress-blocked here, so the headline claim comes from a search snippet only; hardware is null. B rests on the peer-reviewed KDD paper, not on numbers I read. (2) The repo does not carry a timing harness: PFT.cpp prints only the first and last coefficients and the relative L2 error against the MKL full FFT (single precision, DFTI_REAL, not in place) and contains no timers; FFTW.cpp declares clock_t variables but never reads them; src/PrunedFFTW.cpp is the FFTW web-page pseudocode with an unfinished body that does not compile as is. README says MKL code is included in src/ but src/MKL.cpp returns 404, MKL DFTI is inside PFT.cpp. So tier A is impossible from the repo. (3) FFTW baseline in src/FFTW.cpp is a 1,048,576-point float r2c transform with 4 threads planned with FFTW_ESTIMATE (the FFTW_MEASURE alternative is only a comment), a weaker plan than a tuned FFTW; FFTW.cpp includes the Windows-only tchar.h. (4) Last commit date and the README-only nature of the last two commits (last substantive source commit is 'Update PFT.cpp', 2021-06-03) were read from the github.com commits page via WebFetch. (5) A later multidimensional follow-up exists (snudatalab/Auto-MPFT, KDD 2024) and may be a better-documented entry; its repo was not opened.

name: SpFFT (sparse-input 3D FFT)
baseline: FFTW (dense 3D FFT) and cuFFT (implied; no comparison is published)
workload: No benchmarked workload. Design target: 3D FFT of sparse frequency-domain data with spherical cutoff, as in plane-wave electronic-structure codes, with MPI slab and pencil decomposition and CUDA or ROCm backends.
claimed_speedup: none: no numbers or speedup claim appear in the README, docs/source details.rst, index.rst, examples.rst or tests/programs/benchmark.cpp
stars_or_usage: 56 stars, 16 forks; conda-forge package; README says it was written for computational materials-science codes with spherical cutoff data (lead names SIRIUS, not verified here)
tradeoffs: Not a new FFT kernel: the 1D transforms are done by FFTW, MKL or cuFFT underneath, and the gain comes from skipping z-columns that are all zero in frequency space and exploiting Hermitian symmetry for R2C and C2R. Needs a precomputed list of non-zero columns, sizes best of the form 2^a 3^b 5^c 7^d, optional MPI, OpenMP, CUDA 11+ or ROCm 5+; C++17, with C and Fortran interfaces; pre-allocated Grid objects are reused between transforms.
caveats: Tier D: I found no numeric comparison against any recognizable baseline. tests/programs/benchmark.cpp (CLI11 plus rt_graph timing, runs only SpFFT transforms with JSON output) contains no FFTW, cuFFT or dense reference, and docs/source/details.rst and README.md state no speed numbers. Published performance data for SpFFT, if any (for example in the SIRIUS or material-science code papers), is behind egress-blocked hosts (readthedocs, doi.org, arXiv) and was not checked. Notability is limited (56 stars) but the project is a dependency of plane-wave DFT codes per its own description. Last commit date was read from the github.com commits page via WebFetch (latest tag mentioned there: release v1.1.1, 2025-01-19).

name: gpuNUFFT
baseline: CPU NUFFT libraries (FINUFFT, NFFT); none benchmarked in any opened page
workload: GPU gridding / NUFFT of arbitrary 2D and 3D non-Cartesian MRI k-space data (MATLAB mex and Python bindings). No benchmark workload found.
claimed_speedup: none: README states no numbers or speedup claim
compiler_and_flags: CUDA Toolkit, CMake 2.8+; README notes it was tested with CUDA 5.0 and gcc 4.6; a later commit adds CUDA 11 support
stars_or_usage: 85 stars, 37 forks; used as the gpunufft backend of pysap-mri and MRI-NUFFT
tradeoffs: Needs an NVIDIA GPU and CUDA; built primarily around MATLAB mex files (MATLAB required unless the Python bindings are used); NUFFT only (gridding with Kaiser-Bessel style kernels), not a general FFT replacement; single precision.
caveats: Tier D: no speed numbers anywhere I could open. README gives install steps only; the LICENSE file cites Knoll et al., ISMRM 2014 p4297 (a conference abstract I did not open) and 'Supporting material' presentations on Dropbox (not opened). mind-inria/mri-nufft-benchmark (opened) benchmarks gpunufft against finufft, cufinufft, ducc0, pynfft and torchkbnufft but commits no results (output is gitignored, no releases, branches main and v2 only), so it holds no independent numbers; the MRI-NUFFT JOSS paper (joss.theoj.org, 10.21105/joss.07743) and MRI-NUFFT docs on github.io are egress-blocked here. Published third-party comparisons (for example a cuFINUFFT paper) were not checked and the direction of any result is unknown to me. LICENSE is MIT plus an added request to credit the author and cite the ISMRM abstract in academic work, so treat as MIT with an attribution request. Baselines FFTW, MKL FFT and KissFFT in the assignment are not what gpuNUFFT is compared with in the MRI literature; the relevant incumbents are CPU NUFFTs. Last commit date was read from the github.com commits page via WebFetch.

name: fbcuda / fbfft (archived)
workload: Batched small power-of-two 1D and 2D FFTs on GPU as used for FFT-based convolution layers of CNNs (paper: Vasilache et al., 'Fast Convolutional Nets With fbfft: A GPU Performance Evaluation', ICLR 2015, arXiv 1412.7580), versus cuFFT.
claimed_speedup: fbfft provides significant speedups over cuFFT (over 1.5x) for the sizes of interest in whole CNNs; WebSearch snippet of the paper also reported an overall mean speedup of 1.51x with standard deviation 0.21 and geometric mean 1.49x. Snippet only: not on any page I opened.
stars_or_usage: 284 stars, 57 forks; repository archived by Facebook on 2020-03-03 (read-only)
tradeoffs: Single-precision float only; power-of-two sizes only (fbfft1D asserts size <= 256, fbfft2D works with a 2^k basis where right and bottom padding fills up to 2^k); real-input batched transforms with fixed templated kernels, so it targets small FFTs (the 'sizes of interest' for convnets), not large single transforms; headers only (.cuh) built with CUDA and Facebook's DeviceTensor utilities; no Python or C ABI. BSD plus an 'Additional Grant of Patent Rights Version 2' (PATENTS file) with a termination clause on patent assertions against Facebook; that grant is non-standard and not OSI-approved, so legal review is advised before copying.
caveats: (1) Numbers are snippet only: arXiv, ar5iv, Semantic Scholar, ResearchGate and techenablement.com are egress-blocked here, so I could not read the paper's tables, the GPU model (from memory the paper used a Tesla K40m; unverified), the cuFFT version, or whether the 1.51x mean is for FFT kernels alone or for whole convolutions. B rests on the peer-reviewed ICLR 2015 paper. (2) The fbcuda repo carries only the kernels: fbfft/ holds FBFFT.cuh, FBFFT-inl.cuh, FBFFT2D-inl.cuh, FBIFFT2D-inl.cuh, FFT2D32.cuh, FFTIteratedConvolution.cuh, Twiddles.cuh, FBFFTCommon.cuh, FBFFTParameters.h; there is no cuFFT comparison or benchmark driver in it (the root has only unrelated perf tests such as IntegerDivisionPerfTest.cu and the KernelTimer helper), and a grep of the opened docs and fbfft sources found no mention of cuFFT or a speedup. The benchmark driver used for the paper is not in this repo; it may live in a sister repo (not opened, unverified). So tier A is not available from this repo. (3) 2014-2015 GPUs and cuFFT versions; modern cuFFT (and cuDNN's FFT or Winograd paths) may have closed the gap. (4) cuFFT is not one of the assignment's baselines (FFTW, MKL FFT, KissFFT); recorded honestly as a GPU baseline with baseline_in_list false. (5) Last commit date and archive date were read from the github.com pages via WebFetch.
